OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $G$ be the graph with vertex set those pairs $(x,y)\in \mathbb{N}^2$ with $\mathrm{gcd}(x,y)=1$, in which we join two vertices if the differ in only one coordinate, and there by $\pm 1$.
Is there a path going to infinity on $G$, say $P$, such that for all $(x,y)\in P$ both $\min(x,y)>1$ and at least one of $x$ or $y$ is composite?
#1212: [Er80,p.114]
number theory | 
primes
Herzog and Stewart studied the graph $G$, which they called visible lattice points, and proved that there is only one infinite component, and conjectured that if $p$ is prime and $p\nmid a$ then $(a,p)$ always belongs to the infinite component. (This is according to [Er80]; I can find no such results of Herzog and Stewart, who have a paper [HeSt71] on which finite patterns appear in the set of visible lattice points, but does not address this question.)
Erdős originally asked this question with just the condition that $\min(x,y)>1$ and (as he recounts in [Er80]) 'foolishly offered 25 dollars for a proof. In the evening Stewart gave the simple proof: $(p_k,p_{k+1})$ can be joined to $(p_{k+1},p_{k+2})$'. Indeed, if $p_k$ is the $k$th prime then there is a path\[(p_k,p_{k+1})\to (p_k,p_{k+1}+1)\to \cdots \]\[\to (p_{k},p_{k+2})\to (p_{k}+1,p_{k+2})\to (p_{k+1},p_{k+2}).\]This is permissible provided $[p_{k+1},p_{k+2}]$ contains no multiple of $p_k$, which is true provided $p_{k+2}<2p_{k}$, which is true for all $k\geq 4$.
One could further demand that the path be monotone (i.e. every step increases the distance from the origin). Is there a monotone path where we change direction after a bounded number of steps?
The first $50\times 50$ block of the graph $G$ restricted to those vertices $(x,y)$ with both $x,y>1$ and at least one of $x$ or $y$ composite is shown here.

 ## An elementary mixed-modulus determinant observation
While working on Erdős Problem #1212, I came across the following simple determinant observation. It is not a solution of the problem, and I make no priority claim. The problem remains open. If this formulation has appeared before, I would be very grateful for a reference.
### Statement
Let $d\ge1$, and put
$$
k=\binom{d+2}{2}-1.
$$
Let
$$
P_0,P_1,\ldots,P_N\in[-B,B]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2,
$$
where $B\ge1$ and $N\ge k$.
For each $1\le i\le N$, suppose that an integer $r_i\ge2$ satisfies
$$
P_i\equiv P_0\pmod{r_i}
$$
coordinatewise. The modulus may vary with $i$; the $r_i$ need not be distinct or pairwise coprime.
Assume that for every distinct $i_1,\ldots,i_k\in{1,\ldots,N}$,
$$
\prod_{j=1}^k r_{i_j}>
\left(2\sqrt{k}B^d\right)^k.
$$
Then all the points $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ lie in the zero set of a nonzero polynomial of total degree at most $d$.
### Proof
List the $k$ nonconstant monomials $m$ in two variables of total degree at most $d$, and form the integer matrix
$$
Z_{i,m}=m(P_i)-m(P_0),\qquad 1\le i\le N.
$$
Every entry in row $i$ is divisible by $r_i$. Hence every $k\times k$ minor formed from rows $i_1,\ldots,i_k$ is divisible by
$$
\prod_{j=1}^k r_{i_j}.
$$
On the other hand, each row has Euclidean norm at most $2\sqrt{k}B^d$, so Hadamard's inequality gives
$$
\left|\det Z_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}\right|
\le
\left(2\sqrt{k}B^d\right)^k.
$$
By the strict inequality above, every such minor must be zero. Hence $\operatorname{rank}(Z)<k$.
It follows that there is a nonzero $Q\in\mathbb Q[X,Y]$, with no constant term and degree at most $d$, such that
$$
Q(P_i)=Q(P_0)
$$
for every $i$. Therefore
$$
Q(X,Y)-Q(P_0)
$$
is a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $d$ vanishing on all the points.
The determinant method itself is classical. The useful feature here is the row-wise hypothesis: row $i$ contributes its own modulus $r_i$, rather than requiring one common modulus for the whole point set.
### Why this came up in #1212
In a hypothetical long dual blocker contour, a blocker associated with a given lane may carry a large prime witness. If distinct lanes provide sufficiently large row-wise witnesses, the lemma compresses a long collection of blocker points into a low-degree algebraic curve.
The hope is to combine this compression with integral-point bounds to show that such a contour is too sparse to separate a large rectangle.
For this application, one additionally needs to choose one blocker on each of pairwise distinct lanes or columns. That is an application condition, not a hypothesis of the abstract determinant lemma.
This is only a local compression mechanism. The missing global step for #1212 is to produce one compatible rooted contour or crossing at arbitrarily large scales. In particular, the lemma does **not** prove the existence of an infinite path.
### Relation to existing partial work
Existing partial work on #1212 includes the roughness and composite-anchored leg lemmas in Formal Conjectures PR #4218, as well as Ephraim Duncan's drift obstruction showing that any qualifying infinite path must move arbitrarily far from the diagonal.
These seem complementary to the row-wise determinant observation above. I have not found this lemma in either source, but pointers to prior art are very welcome.
I would especially welcome:
1. a citation for the mixed-modulus lemma in this form;
2. variants with better geometric height bounds;
3. applications where row-specific congruence witnesses force algebraic structure.

 I've machine-checked some structural observations on this problem in Lean 4 + Mathlib; all statements and axiom receipts are at https://github.com/ephraimduncan/erdos-1212.
The main one is a drift obstruction: no qualifying path stays within bounded distance of the diagonal. If a walk through qualifying vertices satisfies $|y-x| \le D$ at every vertex, it is confined to a box of explicit size $2 \cdot D! \cdot (x_0+1) + D$, where $x_0$ is the starting abscissa. So any path going to infinity has $\limsup |y-x| = \infty$ (formalized as "exceeds every bound infinitely often").
Proof sketch. The walk can never change sides of the diagonal, since each step changes $y - x$ by $\pm 1$ and offset $0$ is impossible ($\gcd(x,x) = x > 1$). So assume $0 < y - x \le D$ throughout. Let $m = D! \cdot (x_0 + 1)$ and look at the first step with $x > m$. It would have to leave some vertex $(m, m+d)$ with $1 \le d \le D$, going east. For $d \ge 2$ we have $d \mid D! \mid m$, so $\gcd(m, m+d) \ge d > 1$ and $(m, m+d)$ was never a vertex to begin with. For $d = 1$, the east step lands on the diagonal point $(m+1, m+1)$, which is not a vertex either. So $x \le m$ forever. $\square$
Nothing in the argument uses more than coprimality, so it applies just as well to the original 1979 version of the problem. In particular it quantifies why Stewart's prime-pair path needs unbounded prime gaps.
Two smaller facts, both also formalized:
- No finite obstruction. Qualifying paths of every finite length exist, e.g. the column $x = P^2$ at heights $2 \le y \le P - 1$ for any prime $P$ (coprimality is automatic below $P$, and $P^2$ is composite). So the answer cannot be settled negatively by a finite computation near the origin.
- Isolated vertices. For twin primes $p, p+2$, the vertex $(p, p+1)$ has no neighbours at all in the qualifying subgraph: $(p, p+2)$ is a prime pair, $(p-1, p+1)$ is an even pair, and the other two neighbours sit on the diagonal. A concrete instance is $(3, 4)$.
On prior art: the closed formal-conjectures PR #4218 (https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/4218, June 2026) formalizes the statement, proves conditional composite-anchored leg lemmas that anticipate the elevator observation, and describes further unpublished partial results in the same direction. Vardi's Deterministic percolation (1999) constructs isolated vertices in the unrestricted visible-lattice graph. I could not find the drift obstruction above in any source, including that PR; corrections and pointers to prior art are very welcome.
Computationally (there is a reproduction script in the repo), the qualifying subgraph fragments into small finite components near the origin, e.g. the component of $(9,10)$ is exactly $\{(9,10), (9,11), (10,11), (8,11)\}$, but it appears to percolate at coordinates $\gtrsim 10^3$, and the explored paths do drift away from the diagonal, as the theorem says they must. The computations suggest the answer is yes, via unbounded drift, though nothing here proves it; the problem of course remains open.

A full proof 
claimed by Alex Chengyu Li (using Proof Engine (https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7237460; https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22346064), with ChatGPT 5.6 and ChatGPT 6 Astra).
 Summary:
 I prove that the composite-restricted visible lattice contains an infinite simple path, answering Problem 1212 affirmatively. More precisely, for Lebesgue-almost every $\alpha\in(4/3,5/3)$, there is such a path with $x_n/y_n\to\alpha$. The key step associates a bounded-height integer polynomial to a localized bad crossing, using large common prime divisors to force a polynomial evaluation to vanish. Summable exceptional-direction estimates then give safe crossings in narrowing corridors. Connecting these crossings across dyadic scales and extracting a simple ray gives the claimed infinite path and limiting direction.
 Notes:
 Formalization was completed after the linked Zenodo version. The original problem and the displayed main theorem are kernel-checked in Lean using only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. The linked public repository contains the formalization, current manuscript, audit output and versioned release v1.0.0.
